title: Hamming Codes: Detecting and Correcting Errors in Binary Streams

sections.title: The Problem: Bit Flips
sections.teaches: Understanding that noise in transmission channels can flip bits, necessitating error detection.
sections.visual: A binary string '1011' appears on the left. A red lightning bolt strikes the second bit, flipping it to '0'. The string becomes '0011' and shakes slightly to indicate corruption.
sections.narration: Imagine sending a simple message through a noisy channel. Sometimes, interference causes bits to flip unexpectedly, turning your data into garbage upon arrival.

sections.title: The Solution: Parity Bits
sections.teaches: Introducing Hamming codes by adding parity bits at power-of-two positions to create redundancy.
sections.visual: Slots for data bits (D1, D2, D3) and parity bits (P1, P2, P4) appear. The bits are arranged in a sequence: P1, D1, P2, D2, P4, D3. Green checkmarks highlight that each parity bit covers specific positions.
sections.narration: To fix this, we add extra 'parity' bits at specific positions. These redundant bits allow us to verify the integrity of the original data by checking if certain groups of bits have an even or odd number of ones.

sections.title: The Mechanism: Syndrome Calculation
sections.teaches: Explaining how mismatched parity checks create a binary 'syndrome' that points to the error location.
sections.visual: Three circles representing P1, P2, and P4 overlap like a Venn diagram over the data bits. When an error occurs in D2, the circles for P1 and P4 light up red (fail), while P2 stays green (pass). The binary result '101' (decimal 5) highlights position 5.
sections.narration: If a parity check fails, it contributes a '1' to a special code called the syndrome. By combining these results, we get a binary number that directly points to the exact location of the corrupted bit.

sections.title: The Correction: Flipping Back
sections.teaches: Demonstrating the final step of flipping the identified bit to restore the original message.
sections.visual: The binary string shows '0011' with position 5 highlighted in red. An arrow points to this bit, which flips from '0' back to '1'. The string becomes '0010', and a large green 'CORRECTED' stamp appears over it.
sections.narration: The syndrome tells us exactly which bit is wrong. We simply flip that bit back, restoring the original message perfectly. This is the power of Hamming codes: detecting and correcting single-bit errors automatically.
